# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Expanse - Unlock wasted GPU capacity", 2026-05-04 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QCF-expanse-unlock-wasted-gpu-capacity
- [HN] Launch HN: "Launch HN: Expanse (YC P26) – Unlock Wasted GPU Capacity", 2026-06-01, the founders' post and the thread (27 comments), read whole through the HN Algolia API — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48356312 (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48356312)
- [WB] expanse.sh as archived 2026-06-01, the day of the Launch HN — https://web.archive.org/web/20260601142950/https://expanse.sh/
- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/expanse
- [SITE] expanse.sh, read 2026-10-22 — https://expanse.sh

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

Researchers (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Priyanka Raghunathan → [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work"; the fine-tuning run is the author's.

- Kwabena Owusu → author's invention, filling a gap: an ML engineer whose sizes come from past runs on a dashboard, so the problem is not a chorus (against on Importance and Current solution).
- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention: a chipped (rather_not_say) story at a quant fund, GUESSED by code.
- Rafael Moreno → author's invention: a vague, habitual story (GUESSED), echoing [HN] "everyone over-requests by two to three times".
- Ingrid Haugen → author's invention: a gate No (writing up, no jobs that week).
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention: a gate No (away at a conference).
- Yusuf Demir → [HN] "snooping on sumbit scripts ... many of them are egregiously bad": a copied script holding eight GPUs.
- Claire Dubois-Martin → author's invention, filling a gap: a licensed binary with no source code, so the tested condition fails ('no').
- Hiroshi Takeda → [HN] "at least for everyone else, I'd would prefer tuning my own usage myself": he profiles a test run (Current solution mostly works; Adoption friction no).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → [HN] "you lose days of work"; the walltime limit and the group allocation are the author's.
- Diego Castañeda → [HN] the student's PDE simulation ("If I'm running a PDE simulation, and I allocate n machines I want to use all of them"); he keeps his margin (Adoption friction probably not).

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.
- Leilani Kahale → [HN] "In many places the cost of the HPC hardware isn't passed onto them": a grant-funded university cluster that does not measure the waste (dont_know) and has no line for a monthly fee.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

founder.order_why: It runs from naming and market to context, problem, solution, then pilot and distribution, which is how I'd explain Expanse to anyone, so nothing feels out of place.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the same question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.') with only the recency screen between them, so they read as the same question asked twice even if they fill different fields.
founder.missing: The commercial side of Expanse is never asked. Nothing asks who pays: the cluster operator, per cluster, with a department running the pilot rather than the researcher who submits jobs. Nothing asks the price (per cluster a month) or what it is set against, the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and never used. Nothing asks what stands in the way of buying, chiefly a security review of an agent on every node that reads job scripts and source code. There is also no way to send the questions to operators as a second group alongside the researchers, which is where my willingness-to-pay question lives.

PRIMARY.order_why: The question about whether my source code was on the cluster comes after the idea card even though it's about my last job, so it reads like a Part 1 question stranded in Part 2 and breaks the flow from the idea into whether it would have helped.
PRIMARY.missing: What actually happened when the job went over its request (killed mid-run, how much work or how many days I lost), and how much I usually pad memory, GPUs and time when I guess them before submitting.

screens.instead: What does it do better than the way they do it today? Belief: For most, their last job would have gone better with it: it runs first time with no resubmits, and the smaller request waits less in the queue.

screens.why1: Right after I said what it does better, Keel shows the benefits it drafted from my answer so I can check them before they go to researchers, so this screen clearly belongs here.
screens.why2: "Runs first time, no resubmits" and "a shorter wait in the queue" are how anyone on a SLURM or K8s cluster talks about their jobs.
screens.why3: A researcher knows whether their last job died and had to be resubmitted, and how long it sat in the queue, so both benefits come from their own week.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and in the trade's words, but the one my launch leads with is missing: not having to guess memory, GPUs and walltime before submitting; a researcher who values that would find no row to tick.
screens.why5: The rows keep my "debug failures in seconds, not days" and the queue-wait reading, the test sits on the first, and nothing about the agent, the operator or the price leaks to the researcher.
screens.instead: Rows: The job runs first time, no resubmits / A shorter wait in the queue / No guessing memory, GPUs or run time

screens.why1: After the fit and the advantage, asking what a researcher has to do to start using it is the obvious next part of the solution, and it is the last of the four.
screens.why2: Setup, extra steps or learning is plain to me, and padding and suggested sizes are how my researchers talk about job requests.
screens.why3: I know exactly what we ask of a researcher: trust the predicted VRAM, GPUs and walltime instead of the usual 2-3x pad, and apply the line-level fixes if they want.
screens.why4: It is a free box with one escape chip, and 'Leave this out of the study' fits a founder who has nothing to add here.
screens.why5: The belief keeps 'use the suggested sizes instead of padding' word for word but silently drops my second step, applying the line-level code fixes.
screens.instead: What will a researcher have to do to start using it? (e.g. submit with the suggested sizes instead of padding; apply the code fixes it flags) -- and show both steps in the belief, or say which one is tested.

screens.why1: It comes right after I said what researchers will have to do to start using it, so checking Keel's draft of those steps belongs here.
screens.why2: 'Padding' and 'line-level code fixes' are how I and my researchers talk about over-requesting and the profiler's suggestions.
screens.why3: I know exactly what a researcher has to change: take our predicted VRAM, GPUs and walltime instead of the 2-3x pad, and optionally apply the code fixes.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and they cover the researcher's side, because they submit through SLURM or K8s as before; the node agent is the operator's install, not theirs.
screens.why5: Both rows and the belief 'Most would use the suggested sizes instead of padding' are what I typed, and testing the sizes over the code fixes is the right pick.

screens.why1: Right after I named the two things a researcher has to do to start, it is obvious that Keel asks which one is most likely to stop them so it can spend its one question there.
screens.why2: "Suggested sizes", "padding" and "line-level code fixes" are exactly how I and my researchers talk about over-requesting and the optimisations we surface, and the intro says plainly what the pick does.
screens.why3: As the founder I know from the thread that the real fear is a killed job, so trusting our sizes over their own padding is the effort I believe stops them, and I can judge that from what I see.
screens.why4: The two options are the two efforts I typed, distinct and in my words, and with only my own items there is no missing or odd one and no escape chip is needed.
screens.why5: The belief and test, "Most would use the suggested sizes instead of padding", are my item verbatim, with nothing reworded, and the 1-in-3 bar is a fair line for it.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out is the obvious point to decide whether strangers who like it get asked to try it, and I'm onboarding paid pilots, so I want those names.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with the hint quoting the exact closing line and pointing to the Pilot tab reads at once; "pilot" is my own word for how we sell.
screens.why3: Whether I want sign-ups from this study is purely my call and I know the answer: yes, every warm cluster contact counts.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the whole decision, the two chips are distinct, and the Continue button echoes my pick.
screens.why5: The quoted line "Would you try this for real?" doesn't promise my paid per-cluster pilot terms or leak anything, so it fits what I'd say to a stranger.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out to researchers, choosing who will ask them the questions is an obvious last step, and it follows the pilot offer naturally.
screens.why2: The hint packs video, voice, typing, a 400-credit recording charge and text-message delivery into one block, and it says Keel records 'the voice' while the interviewer is on video, so I have to read it twice to know whether I'm picking a face, a voice or both.
screens.why3: I can play two 5-second clips and pick the one I'd want talking to an ML engineer about their SLURM jobs, so this is entirely my call.
screens.why4: Two names with a play button are distinct and the preselected default works as the escape, but the cards don't say whether a face comes with the voice, and there's no plain option to send the questions as text only, which some of my researchers would prefer.
screens.why5: It asks who should question 'researchers', my own word, and nothing about Expanse or the operator buyer shows through to the people being asked.
screens.instead: Who should ask researchers your questions on video? (They can also read each question and type or tap.) — Daphne ▶ 5 s / Saskia ▶ 5 s; recording your pick costs 400 credits either way.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, picking how researchers answer is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but the Daphne option is crowded with a recognition-accuracy claim and status chips ('Still recording', 'Ready when Daphne is') that take a second read.
screens.why3: I know my researchers: they live in terminals and Slack, would rather read and tap than talk to a video, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: AI voice, text, or let them choose covers the real choices and they are distinct; the readiness labels make the trade-off clear.
screens.why5: Nothing about my product or roles is distorted; it is a delivery choice and 'researchers' is my own word.
screens.instead: How should researchers answer? — Read and tap (ready now) / AI interviewer on video, Daphne (ready in a few minutes) / Let them choose

screens.why1: After choosing how researchers answer, deciding who gets a link is the obvious last step before sending the study out.
screens.why2: The three choices are plain, but the first option's label runs into its description without a break ("People I know by name I send each one...") and needs a second read, and "the Contacts page" names a part of Keel I have not seen yet.
screens.why3: I know who I will reach first, the researchers on the HPC and GPU clusters I have talked to, so I can answer from what I already do.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my real cases, a named list or an open link posted where researchers already gather, but the open link's Google sign-in is odd for researchers on institutional SSO, and there is no option to combine named people with an open link.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes what I typed about Expanse, and nothing about the product or the roles leaks onto the screen.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name: you send each one their own link · A list from Keel's Contacts search: Keel makes a link for each, you send them · One open link to post where researchers already are (a Slack, a mailing list, a forum); each person signs in before the interview

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside the deciding number on every card: 4 answered, 5 needed to call it.
screens.why_b2: The bar of 5 and the 4 counted are plain, but the kicker says 7 people answered while each card counts 4, and nothing says why 3 dropped out, so I had to look twice.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction carry the exact belief lines I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need more answers, but the screen never says to get one more counted researcher per belief or what that means for the pilot pitch.
screens.why_b5: Nothing is claimed beyond the 4 counted; the low n is stated plainly and no belief is called held.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 7 researchers answered, but only 4 got to these questions (3 said they ran no jobs that week); get at least one more who did, and each belief can be called.

screens.why_b3: 'Compatibility' and 'For most researchers, the source code sat on the cluster' are word for word what I checked.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is true, but it doesn't say the obvious next step: every counted answer is for me, so one more real answer from a researcher would settle it.
screens.why_b5: It honestly calls this 'a lean, not a call', but the verdict says '4 answered' while the count line says '5 answered · 4 counted', which blurs who actually answered.

screens.why_b3: Relative advantage and 'the job runs first time, no resubmits' are exactly the belief I checked on the way in.

screens.why1: A screener asking whether I run jobs on a big shared GPU cluster is the obvious first gate for a study about my cluster work.
screens.why2: Jobs, cluster and GPUs are my everyday words, and I can answer it on first reading.
screens.why3: I submit to our shared cluster every day, but I'd have to guess whether it counts as 100 or more GPUs, since I see my partition and quota more than the total size.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it cleanly for a screener with no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment of 100 or more GPUs and leaks nothing of a product or plan.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and the two options are easy to hold, though 'I'll read 2 options' is a bit stiff for a plain yes or no.
screens.instead: Do you submit jobs to a shared GPU cluster with 100 or more GPUs in total? Yes; or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I run on a 100-plus GPU cluster, asking whether a job of mine blew past what I asked for this week is the obvious next filter for the story.
screens.why2: Exceeding the resource request is plain SLURM talk to me, even if I'd say it got OOM-killed or hit its walltime.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether a job of mine died on memory or time this week, because I'm the one who resubmitted it.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but a gate shouldn't carry an escape at all, and here it has two chips, one of them the banned 'I'd rather not say'.
screens.why5: The founder's situation is guessing memory, GPUs and time before submitting, and 'exceed' narrows that to under-requesting, missing jobs where I over-reserved and wasted the cluster.
screens.why6: One short question ending in 'Yes or no' is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did one of your jobs run out of memory or hit its time limit? Yes / No (no escape chip on the gate)

screens.why1: Right after asking whether a job of mine blew past its request, showing a tool that predicts what a job needs at submit time is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: SLURM, walltime, GPU memory and submission script are my everyday words, but 'a prediction of job resources' is a clumsy way to name a tool, and 'flags failures' leaves me unsure if it means predicted failures or ones that already happened.
screens.why3: I guess memory, GPUs and walltime on every sbatch I write, so I can judge this from my own runs.
screens.why4: A card to read with no options.
screens.why5: The idea is shown on purpose as an Imagine card, and the belief line points back to the submit-time prediction instead of re-listing features, so nothing leaks where it shouldn't.
screens.why6: It is seven sentences heard in one go, and 'GPU memory, memory, CPUs and walltime' plus 'suggests line-level optimisations' are a mouthful to hold by ear.
screens.instead: Imagine Expanse, a tool that tells you what a job needs before you submit it. It runs on your own cluster, reads your code, script and hardware, and predicts GPU memory, memory, CPUs and walltime. If a job fails, it tells you why and how to fix it. The people building it believe it would tell you, at submit time, what each job actually needs.

screens.why1: It plausibly checks whether a resource predictor could read my code, but straight after the idea card it lands abruptly, since nothing says why my code's location matters.
screens.why2: Source code, cluster and last job are my everyday words, so I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know where my code was for my last job; it was a git clone in my home directory on the cluster.
screens.why4: Yes, with some steps is odd for a plain past fact, since my code either was on the cluster or was not, though I could read it as having to sync or copy it over first.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks, but it has likely drifted a little from what the predictor needs, which is probably my job script and code being readable by a tool rather than merely sitting on the cluster.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, three short options and one escape, all easy to hold when heard once.
screens.instead: Think of your last job. Were its code and submission script on the cluster where a tool could read them? Yes; yes, after copying them over; or no. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the question about my last job, it's obvious they want to know whether a resource prediction would have helped that job.
screens.why2: I understand it on first read, but 'go better' is vague: I'd have to decide whether it means not getting OOM-killed, not timing out, or not hogging GPUs I didn't need.
screens.why3: I know how my last job went, but whether a prediction would have beaten my own guess at memory and walltime is partly a guess, since I only have a one-line idea card to go on.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover it cleanly, and 'I can't tell' is the right escape for something I'm imagining.
screens.why5: The founder's aim is a job that runs to the end without wasting the cluster, and 'go better for you' drifts from that into a general feeling, though nothing of the product leaks beyond the card.
screens.why6: Short, one question, four short options I can hold, and one escape said last; it says well.
screens.instead: Would Expanse's guess at memory, GPUs and run time have got your last job to finish without over-reserving, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After asking whether it would have helped my last job, asking whether I'd actually trust its sizes over my own padding is the natural last question.
screens.why2: Padding requests is exactly how we talk about it on the cluster, and suggested sizes is clear enough on first read.
screens.why3: I pad every submission because under-requesting kills my run, so I know exactly how I'd feel about dropping that.
screens.why4: Yes and Yes, if it was clearly worth it overlap for me, and the real condition is whether a wrong guess would kill my job, which none of the options names.
screens.why5: It keeps the idea as a sizing suggestion that replaces padding, with no product terms or roles leaking beyond the shown card.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold after one hearing, with one escape at the end.
screens.instead: To use Expanse, you'd request its suggested sizes instead of padding. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Yes, but only for short or cheap jobs · Only if a bad guess couldn't kill my job · No; escape: I can't tell
